ruleIntents.intent: Checks a non-embedded HTML page has a programmatically present non-empty title: the root html element must have a descendant title element, and the first title in document order must contain non-whitespace text. Pure presence and non-emptiness check; does not test whether the title is descriptive or meaningful.
ruleIntents.scLimb: Exercises only the page-has-a-title limb of SC 2.4.2, not the title-describes-topic-or-purpose limb. Operationalizes title-present as a title element under the root html with non-whitespace text in its first occurrence.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to the page root only when it is an html element (non-embedded HTML document). Inapplicable when the root is not html (e.g. a standalone svg root) and when HTML is embedded via iframe or object. Title from a higher-level protocol (email subject) is out of scope by assumption.
ruleIntents.expectation: Both must hold to pass. E1: the root html element has at least one descendant title element. E2: the first title element descendant of the document element has text-node children that are not only whitespace. Fail = no title element, or first title is empty, whitespace-only, or only a separator character.
scenarioTypesPresent: pass: html root with non-empty title directly under html
fail: html root with an h1 but no title element
inapplicable: root is svg not html with an svg title

rule example set: title under head vs body vs html; multiple titles where first non-empty wins and first empty fails; whitespace-only and separator-only titles fail; title in iframe ignored; title in shadow tree ignored; embedded iframe page inapplicable
syntheticNarrowness: 3-4 line trivial pages, no real head metadata, CSS, JS, or content unlike production pages full of meta and framework boilerplate
static source titles only: misses runtime document.title, SPA route title changes, server-templated and post-hydration titles a static DOM snapshot can misjudge

emptiness probed only with whitespace and a separator, never realistic degenerate-but-nonempty titles like Untitled, Document, index, New Tab, site-name-only, lone pipe, NBSP, zero-width, emoji-only, numeric-only, which all pass yet violate the spirit of 2.4.2
ASCII English only: no RTL, CJK, combining marks, or HTML entities to test whitespace and text-node normalization
no computed-title nuance: whitespace after entity decode, multiple text nodes or comments, CDATA, or title content interspersed with elements
scope exclusions (iframe, object, shadow DOM, non-html root) tested in isolation, never combined in a realistic composite document
descriptiveness untested by design, so asdf or Home passes and the corpus gives no signal on the substantive 2.4.2 requirement

ruleIntents.intent: Checks the semantic quality of an HTML page's document title: that the first title element actually describes the topic or purpose of the page's overall content, rather than merely existing or being non-empty. This is a content/meaning judgment (does "Apple harvesting season" describe a page about clementines?), not a structural/presence check. It is explicitly the descriptiveness half of SC 2.4.2 — the companion rule (HTML page has non-empty title) owns the missing/whitespace-only title case, so this rule presumes a non-empty title is present and only asks whether that title is informative.
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 2.4.2 has two conjoined limbs: (a) web pages have titles, and (b) those titles describe topic or purpose. This rule exercises limb (b) — the "that describe topic or purpose" clause — only. Limb (a) (existence/non-emptiness) is deliberately carved out to the related rule and appears here as the Applicability exclusion (no document title / whitespace-only title => inapplicable), not as a failure.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to the document title of each HTML web page — operationally, the first title element of the page (Accessibility Support note: browsers honor only the first title, so the rule scopes itself to that one). Inapplicable when: the page has no document title, OR the document title is whitespace-only, OR the only title is inside an embedded document (svg/iframe/object) since those are not "web pages" per WCAG — the inapplicable corpus case is exactly a bare SVG fragment whose title belongs to the svg, not to an HTML document.
ruleIntents.expectation: The target element (first title) describes the topic or purpose of the overall content of the document. Pass = the first non-empty title is content-descriptive; this holds even when a second title follows (ignored) and even when the title element sits in the body rather than head (browser repairs it). Fail = the first title is non-descriptive: wrong subject vs. the page content, a misleading first-of-two title, or a generic/site-name-only title that names the site but not the specific page.
scenarioTypesPresent: Descriptive title in head matching body content (clear pass)
Descriptive first title with a second title present that is ignored (multiple-title precedence, pass)
Descriptive title element placed in body instead of head (DOM-position tolerance via browser repair, pass)
Title about the wrong subject relative to page content (Apple title / clementine content, fail)
Misleading first of two titles where the correct title is second (first-title-wins precedence, fail)
Generic site-name-only title that does not identify the specific page (search-results page titled only University of Arkham, fail)
Title element belonging to an embedded SVG document rather than an HTML page (inapplicable)
syntheticNarrowness:
All HTML cases reuse one tiny clementine/apple toy domain — a single short

as the entire page content; no real pages with mixed sections, navigation, headings hierarchy, or long-form content where judging topic/purpose is genuinely hard

Descriptiveness signal is almost lexically trivial: pass titles literally contain the body's keyword (Clementine) and the wrong-subject fail swaps one obvious noun (Apple vs Clementine), so the judgment reduces to keyword matching rather than the real semantic question of whether a title summarizes a page

The only nuanced descriptiveness failure (generic site-name-only) is a single canned example (University of Arkham); no coverage of other common real-world generic titles like 'Home', 'Untitled Document', 'index', boilerplate CMS defaults, or titles that are descriptive-but-wrong (describe a different page in the site)

No coverage of titles that are technically present but useless in practice: all-uppercase noise, very long keyword-stuffed SEO titles, titles that are just the URL or a date/ID, or titles in a language different from the page content

Multiplicity/position edge cases are minimal: exactly two titles or one body title; no zero-vs-many beyond that, no title split across elements, no dynamically-injected title (SPA/JS-set document.title), and the missing/whitespace-only inapplicable branch is not even represented here (only the embedded-SVG inapplicable case is)

Embedded-document exclusion is tested with only a standalone SVG fragment; no iframe or object cases, and no realistic page that contains BOTH a proper HTML document title AND embedded svg/iframe titles to confirm the embedded ones are correctly ignored while the HTML one is judged

Language/localization is hard-coded to lang=en with English content and English titles; the rule's Input Aspect 'Language' (judging descriptiveness requires understanding the title's language vs the content) is never exercised with non-English or mismatched-language content

No internationalized, RTL, or multi-byte titles, and no titles that are descriptive via context the title alone can't show (e.g., 'Step 2 of 5') — the corpus avoids every case where human/LLM judgment of 'describes purpose' would be contentious, which is precisely where this manual/semi-auto rule's real difficulty lives

scLimbsCoveredByACT: EXISTENCE of a title mechanism (title present vs. absent). Covered by 2779a5: PASS 7f9f315b (has a <title>) vs. FAIL 820fb18c (only an <h1>, no title). Maps to TT Test 12.A 'A <title> element is defined for the web page' and Understanding 'marked up with the <title> element'.

NON-EMPTY title content (real text vs. empty/whitespace/separator-only). Covered by 2779a5: FAIL 314d991 (empty <title></title>), FAIL 4eeff9c (title is a single space / separator char). Maps to TT 12.A 'Page <title> cannot be empty' and F25 'Empty text'.

DESCRIPTIVE title that identifies topic/purpose (title content matches page content). Covered by c4a8a4: PASS c19c231 ('Clementine harvesting season' over clementine content) vs. FAIL 2c139703 ('Apple harvesting season' over clementine content). This is the core SC text 'titles that describe topic or purpose' and G88 'the title is relevant to the content'.

GENERIC / non-identifying title that is non-empty but does not describe THIS page. Covered by c4a8a4 FAIL 4c72b3b ('University of Arkham' site name only, on a search-results page). Maps to F25 'title does not identify the contents or purpose' and the Understanding note that an org/site name alone need not describe the page.

MULTIPLE <title> elements, first-wins precedence. Covered by 2779a5 (PASS 6b3d2e2 two filled; PASS 0ad882d first filled / second empty; FAIL a149686 first empty / second filled) and c4a8a4 (PASS 107a5e4 first descriptive / second ignored; FAIL 1844d7b first non-descriptive / second descriptive). Tests the ACT 'browsers use the first title element' assumption.

TITLE PLACEMENT variants (in <head>, in <body>, or no <head>). Covered by 2779a5 PASS efa1e04 (title in body), PASS 7f9f315b (title direct child of <html>), and c4a8a4 PASS 2f970957 (title in body). Tests the ACT assumption that a title need not be a child of <head>.

EMBEDDED-DOCUMENT boundary / scope of 'web page'. Covered by 2779a5: PASS 64771c39 (host page titles itself, iframe child untitled), FAIL 5fd6fda (page is iframe-only with no own title; iframe's title does not count), and unapproved 94ff404. Maps to ACT background 'pages embedded via iframe/object are not web pages' and the 2779a5 assumption about higher-level protocols.

INAPPLICABLE: <title> inside a non-HTML-page context (SVG <title>). Covered by both rules: 2779a5 INAPPLICABLE ecc29b7 and c4a8a4 INAPPLICABLE 85469fd ('This is a circle'). Maps to ACT applicability ('applies to the root html element' / 'title elements of svg are not web pages').
SHADOW DOM / scripted title not in the document tree. Covered by unapproved 2779a5 FAIL 9c5eeb53 (title injected into a shadow root, not a descendant of the document element).
scLimbsAbsentFromACT: SET-OF-PAGES / DISTINGUISHABILITY limb. SC text via TT 12.B(2) 'If the web page is part of a set of web pages, the Page Title accurately distinguishes the web page from other pages', F25 'A site generated using templates includes the same title for each page ... cannot be used to distinguish among the pages', and Understanding's whole APG 'set of web pages' example. NO test case is part of a set or tests duplicate/non-unique titles across pages — every case is a single standalone page. This entire limb (uniqueness within a site) is untested.

DYNAMIC / SPA title changes. Understanding: 'in cases such as Single Page Applications (SPAs) ... the title of the page should also be changed dynamically to reflect ... the current view.' No test case has a title that updates on view/route change (the only scripted case, 9c5eeb53, scripts a shadow root, not a title update). Entirely absent.

DOCUMENT / WEB-APPLICATION naming as a sufficient title. Understanding: 'the name of the document or web application would be sufficient to describe the purpose of the page'; TT 12.B(b) repeats this; Understanding's banking-app example ('Bank XYZ, accounts for Alex Smith'). No test case is a document or web application, nor tests an app/document-name title. Absent.

RELATIONSHIP-TO-COLLECTION limb (advisory technique G127). 'Identify the site or other resource to which the web page belongs' (G88) and G127 examples (sub-site name in title, chapter+textbook title, collection metadata via link rel). No test case includes site/sub-site/collection naming, breadcrumb-style titles, or rel-based metadata. Absent.

AUTHORING-TOOL DEFAULT / PLACEHOLDER titles. F25 lists 'Untitled Document', 'No Title', 'Untitled Page', 'New Page 1', 'Enter the title of your HTML document here', non-descriptive filenames (report.html, spk12.html), and 'Filler or placeholder text'. The descriptive-failure case (4c72b3b) is a real org name, not a default/placeholder. None of these classic failure strings appear. Absent.

NON-HTML / OTHER-TECHNOLOGY titling. EN 301 549 C.9.2.4.2 and all three techniques say 'All technologies'; Understanding gives 'A synchronized media presentation about the 2004 ... titled "The Tsunami of 2004"' (G88). Both ACT rules are HTML-only by name. No PDF, no synchronized-media, no non-web-document title is tested. Absent (this is an ACT-rule scope limit, but it is an SC limb).

TITLE-BAR PRESENTATION / user-agent surfacing. Understanding: 'User agents make the title ... easily available ... display the page title in the window title bar or as the name of the tab'; TT/ANDI read the rendered page title. All cases are judged on source <title>; none test the rendered/exposed title (e.g., title overridden by document.title at runtime to something different). Absent.

LANGUAGE / SCRIPT / LENGTH variety of descriptive titles. G88 'Be short'; Understanding shows multi-part titles ('Working with us: The Small Group: The Big Organization'). All descriptive cases use a single short English phrase; no over-long, multi-part, or non-English/RTL descriptive title is tested. Largely absent (length/conciseness limb of G88 untested).

aspects.title: Title is a non-empty but non-identifying artifact: authoring-tool default, unfilled placeholder, or filename/code string
aspects.description: F25 names a family of title strings that are non-empty, valid, and pass the presence rule (2779a5), yet fail 2.4.2 because the string itself identifies nothing about the page's content. Three sub-classes, all requiring semantic recognition that the string is residue rather than content: (a) authoring-tool defaults ('Untitled Document', 'Enter the title of your HTML document here', 'No Title', 'New Page 1'); (b) filler/placeholder/unfilled-template text ('Lorem ipsum', 'TODO: title', 'PAGE TITLE HERE', 'xxxxx', 'test'); (c) filenames or machine identifiers that are not descriptive in their own right ('report.html', 'spk12.html', SKUs, build hashes, Drupal-style 'node/3387', raw slugs like 'page_2_final_v3'). The c4a8a4 descriptiveness corpus contains NONE of these named strings — its only non-descriptive case is a wrong-real-subject title (apple vs clementine) and a site-name-only search page. A checker cannot flag any of these because each is non-empty, valid UTF-8, often dictionary words, and structurally indistinguishable from a legitimate terse title; only semantic recognition that 'Untitled Document' announces no-title, or that '.html' / a hash signals machine residue, catches it.
aspects.scLimb: Limb (b), 'titles that describe topic or purpose' — specifically the F25 case where the title exists and is non-empty but identifies nothing about the page. Limb (a) presence is satisfied and carved out to 2779a5.
aspects.whyUncovered: c4a8a4's failing titles are all natural-language phrases ('Apple harvesting season', 'University of Arkham'); the corpus never presents an authoring default, a placeholder/unfilled-template token, or a filename/code-string title. 2779a5 explicitly passes any non-whitespace title, so 'Untitled Document', 'TODO: title' and 'report.html' sail through both ACT rules. Fully-automated tools cannot distinguish these from a real title: they are non-empty and valid; distinguishing 'report.html' from a genuine 'Report 2024', or 'New Page 1' from a legitimate title, requires understanding that the string is a vestigial tool artifact or unfilled template, not page-identifying content.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build complete, realistic pages (full head metadata, headings, paragraphs, sometimes a data table) whose body has an unambiguous real topic, but whose <title> is a non-identifying artifact string. Rotate across the three sub-classes: authoring-tool default, unfilled placeholder/template token, and filename/code/hash/slug. Each page must be self-contained; the body content must clearly establish the true topic so the artifact title is demonstrably non-identifying. Include F25's own literal examples ('Untitled Document', 'spk12.html', 'report.html') as ground-truth anchors.
suggestedScenarios: A quarterly-revenue article page with rich body (headings, paragraphs, a data table) whose <title> is the literal authoring-tool default 'Untitled Document'.
A finished 'Returns and Refunds Policy' page (full visible <h1> and body) whose <title> is the unfilled CMS token 'TODO: add page title'.
A research summary page with an executive summary and findings whose <title> is literally 'report.html'.
A conference speaker bio page whose <title> is F25's own example 'spk12.html'.
An e-commerce product detail page (product name, price, description in body) whose <title> is the raw SKU 'P-48201-BLK' or the unfilled template token 'PAGE TITLE HERE'.
A completed onboarding-guide page whose <title> is a leftover build slug 'index_a3f9c2_final_v3.html' or a Drupal internal path 'node/3387'.
A real contact-us page (address, map, form) whose <title> is placeholder 'Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet'.

aspects.title: Title describes a secondary/peripheral block instead of the page's primary topic (rich mixed-content pages)
aspects.description:
F25 fails titles that do not identify the contents or purpose of the OVERALL page. On a realistic page with mixed content (a main article plus a sidebar, ad rail, promo banner, related-links, footer tagline), a title can be non-empty and genuinely describe SOMETHING present on the page while completely missing the page's primary subject — e.g. a detailed page about a city budget vote titled after the top promo banner ('Summer Sale - 20% Off'), or a recipe page titled after its sidebar newsletter widget. The c4a8a4 corpus only ever has a single short

as the entire body, so the page's topic is unambiguous by construction and 'which of several content blocks is this page about' is never exercised. Identifying a busy page's PRIMARY topic versus peripheral blocks, and checking the title against the dominant content region, is a quintessential human reading-comprehension/visual-prominence judgment that no presence-or-emptiness checker performs.
aspects.scLimb: Limb (b), 'describe topic or purpose' — the title must identify the OVERALL/primary content of the page, not merely some element that appears on it.
aspects.whyUncovered:
Every c4a8a4 case has one sentence of body content, so there is exactly one possible topic and no competition between primary and peripheral content; the corpus's own syntheticNarrowness admits 'a single short

as the entire page content'. Real pages have headers, sidebars, ads, and related-content rails. Automated tools cannot identify a page's primary topic versus peripheral blocks, have no model of visual or semantic prominence, and do no title-versus-dominant-content comparison; a human must read the page, determine what it is principally about, and judge whether the title names THAT.

references.quote: This describes a failure condition when the web page has a title, but the title does not identify the contents or purpose of the web page.
Identify the subject of the web page
Determine whether the Page Title is a meaningful representation or indication of page content.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build genuinely rich, multi-block pages: a dominant main column (article/recipe/job listing/spec) plus competing peripheral regions (promo banner, sidebar widget, ad/related-item rail, footer tagline, announcement bar). Set the <title> to accurately describe one of the PERIPHERAL blocks so a naive keyword match against the page would still find the title's words present, but a reader who identifies the primary topic sees the title names the wrong region. Vary which peripheral region the title is drawn from.
suggestedScenarios: A long news article about a city budget vote whose <title> is the unrelated top promo banner text 'Summer Sale - 20% Off Subscriptions'.
A recipe page (full ingredients and method as the main column) whose <title> is the sidebar widget's 'Sign up for our newsletter'.
A job-listing page for 'Senior Backend Engineer' (the entire main content) whose <title> is the company's generic mission-statement tagline appearing only in the footer.
A help article on 'Resetting your password' whose <title> describes the top-of-page announcement bar 'Scheduled maintenance Saturday'.
A product spec page whose <title> matches a 'You may also like' related item in the rail rather than the product being viewed.
A page dominated by an Excel-pivot-tables video tutorial whose <title> describes the small 'Featured course' ad in the sidebar.

aspects.title: Stale / copy-paste title: right subject family, wrong specific instance (date, name, version, account)
aspects.description: F25 and Trusted Tester 12.B require the title to accurately identify THIS page. A pervasive real-world failure is a title carried over from a template clone or a prior edit: it is on-topic for the section and looks entirely plausible, but names the wrong specific item — last month's statement title on this month's statement, last year's gala date on this year's event, the donor product's name on a duplicated product page. c4a8a4's 'Apple harvesting season' on a clementine page is the only wrong-subject case, and it is a gross, obvious cross-domain swap (different fruit). The corpus has no subtle in-family mismatch where title and body share the domain and vocabulary but disagree on the specific instance — precisely the case that needs careful human cross-checking of identifiers (date/name/version/number) against the body, and that no presence/emptiness checker, and even a keyword-matcher, can detect (both 'Q3 Report' and a Q4 body contain 'Report').
aspects.scLimb: Limb (b), 'describe topic or purpose' — the title must ACCURATELY identify the specific content of THIS page, not merely be domain-plausible.
aspects.whyUncovered: c4a8a4's single wrong-subject case is a blatant cross-domain topic swap; there is no near-miss where title and content share the domain but differ in the specific instance, date, name, or version. The corpus never models a body that the title must be cross-checked against beyond one obvious sentence. Automated tools do no title-versus-content comparison for descriptiveness at all; even a keyword-overlap tool would pass a stale title that shares vocabulary with the body. Catching it requires reading the body and noticing that the specific identifiers in the title disagree with the page's actual subject.

references.quote: The Page Title accurately identifies the contents or purpose of the web page
the title does not identify the contents or purpose of the web page

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages where the <title> and the body share the same domain and vocabulary but disagree on exactly one critical identifier (date, name, version, account number, model). The body must clearly and specifically establish the true instance (visible dates, account numbers, product specs, images-as-text). The title must be plausible at the category level so only an attentive reader who cross-checks the specific identifier detects the mismatch. Mirror the Understanding bank-statement example pattern (month/account specificity) for one anchor case.
suggestedScenarios: A bank statement page whose body is clearly the 'December 2005 statement for Account 1234-5678' but whose <title> reads 'November 2005 statement for Account 1234-5678' (copy-paste from the prior month).
An event page whose body advertises 'Annual Gala 2026' (date, venue, this-year program) but whose <title> still says 'Annual Gala 2025' (last year's clone).
A product page duplicated from a sibling: <title> 'Stainless Steel Bottle 500ml' while the body, images, specs and price are all for the 750ml model.
A release-notes page whose body is clearly 'Version 4.2.0 release notes' but whose <title> says 'Version 4.1.0 release notes'.
A quarterly report whose <title> is 'Q3 2025 Financial Results' while every figure, heading and date in the body is for Q4 2025.
A staff profile page whose body is entirely 'Dr. Maria Chen, Cardiology' but whose <title> names the previous occupant 'Dr. James Okoro, Cardiology' (template clone).

aspects.title: Title is correct but too generic to distinguish this page from its siblings (site-name-only / template-shared on an inner page)
aspects.description: F25's second example is a distinct failure: 'A site generated using templates includes the same title for each page on the site. So the title cannot be used to distinguish among the pages.' G88 and Trusted Tester 12.B both make distinguish-within-the-set a pass requirement. Here the title may be perfectly accurate about the SITE ('Acme Corporation', 'Online Store', 'Help Center') yet fail 2.4.2 because it carries no page-level information and so cannot distinguish THIS page (Contact) from siblings (Products, About). The single-page-detectable form of this failure — an inner page of an obvious set whose title is only the site name or only the shared template/section label — IS testable on a self-contained HTML page: the body unambiguously reveals the page's specific role, while the title carries only site-level information. Deciding whether 'Acme Corporation' adequately distinguishes the Contact page requires knowing the page's specific role — a human judgment about whether the title carries page-level, not just site-level, information.
aspects.scLimb: Limb (b), 'describe topic or purpose' — within the SC's distinguish-among-a-set requirement: the title must identify THIS page, not merely the site/template it shares with its siblings.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT test cases are single self-contained files with no sibling pages, so 'same title across the set' cannot be encoded; the corpus's only inner-page case is one search page, and c4a8a4's 'University of Arkham' touches site-name-only but as an isolated single page, never as the distinguish-among-siblings problem F25 describes. Fully-automated single-page tools have no cross-page corpus to compare titles against, and even on one page cannot decide whether a site-name-only or template-shared title adequately distinguishes this page's specific role — that requires reading the body to learn the page's role and judging whether the title carries any page-level signal.

references.quote: A site generated using templates includes the same title for each page on the site. So the title cannot be used to distinguish among the pages.
Be unique within the site or other resource to which the web page belongs
If the web page is part of a set of web pages, determine whether the Page Title is sufficient to distinguish the web page from other pages.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build inner pages of an obviously-multi-page site (clear site nav with sibling links present in the page, a footer, a specific <h1> and body) where the body unambiguously establishes a specific page role (Contact, a particular product, a checkout step, a specific article) but the <title> is ONLY the site name or only a shared template/section label that every sibling would also carry. The presence of the nav listing siblings makes the set-membership and the non-distinguishing nature self-evident on the single page. Keep each page self-contained — do not require fetching the siblings.
suggestedScenarios: An inner 'Contact Us' page (form, map, phone in body; nav links to Home/Products/About) whose <title> is only the company name 'Globex Industries'.
A specific product page (body shows 'Stainless Steel Water Bottle 750ml', category nav present) whose <title> is the generic shared 'Online Store'.
A checkout step-3 page (body clearly 'Step 3: Payment', steps 1-2 shown in a progress bar) whose <title> is the same 'Checkout' all steps share.
A knowledge-base article (specific article topic in body, KB nav present) whose <title> is the template default 'Help Center' identical across all articles.
A blog post page whose <title> is just the blog name 'The Daily Byte' rather than the post headline shown in the <h1>.
A documentation page whose body is specifically the 'Authentication API Reference' but whose <title> is only the shared 'Documentation'.

aspects.title: Title is locally descriptive in-page but loses meaning out of context / fails to convey collection position (G88 out-of-context, G127)
aspects.description: G88 makes 'Make sense when read out of context, for example by a screen reader or in a site map or list of search results' a core requirement, and G127 covers titles that identify a page's RELATIONSHIP to a larger collection (its position in a hierarchy, its parent section). A title can be perfectly clear while reading the page ('Chapter 3', 'Settings', 'Step 2', 'GET /users') yet be uninformative when isolated in a list of open tabs, a search-results list, or a screen-reader page list, because it strips all collection/parent context. The Understanding examples model exactly the good pattern ('Alert Dialog Example | APG | WAI | W3C'; 'Bank XYZ, December 2005 statement for Account 1234-5678'). The ACT corpus has no hierarchical or collection-structured cases — every page is a standalone leaf with no parent context — so the 'descriptive in-page but meaningless out of context' failure is never exercised. Judging whether a title 'makes sense out of context' or conveys collection position requires imagining it isolated and understanding the page's role in a larger information architecture — a human contextual judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Limb (b), 'describe topic or purpose' — the title must identify the page in a way that orients the user, including when read out of context, per G88/G127; a context-dependent fragment does not.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus has no multi-level or collection-structured examples; the richest is a flat search-results page, and every case is a standalone leaf with no parent/hierarchy modeled. It never tests a title that is locally descriptive but loses meaning out of context. Automated tools cannot judge whether a title 'makes sense out of context' or conveys collection position — that requires understanding the page's role in a larger information architecture and imagining the title isolated in a list of tabs or search hits; 'Chapter 3' is fine in-page but uninformative as a standalone title, and only a human weighs that.

references.quote: Make sense when read out of context, for example by a screen reader or in a site map or list of search results
to enable users to identify the relationship between the current web page and other web pages in the same collection
Specific examples for each pattern are pages titled "X Example | APG | WAI | W3C" (e.g., "Alert Dialog Example | APG | WAI | W3C")

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages that belong to an evident hierarchy or collection (a textbook chapter, a multi-section settings area, a wizard step, an API-docs endpoint) where the body provides all the local context (e.g. 'Step 2 of 4: Shipping Address', 'Notification Settings', the textbook and chapter name) but the <title> is reduced to the bare context-dependent fragment ('Step 2', 'Settings', 'Chapter 3') that would be meaningless in a list of tabs or search results. Make the in-page clarity vs out-of-context emptiness contrast explicit by having the body name the full context the title omits.
suggestedScenarios: An online-textbook page whose body is clearly chapter 3 of a named physics textbook but whose <title> is just 'Chapter 3' (no book or topic name).
A multi-section settings page whose body is specifically the 'Notification Settings' subsection but whose <title> is only 'Settings'.
A wizard page whose body shows 'Step 2 of 4: Shipping Address' but whose <title> is just 'Step 2'.
An API-docs page whose <title> is just the endpoint name 'GET /users' with no product or section, indistinguishable from another product's identical endpoint.
A forum action page whose <title> is just 'Reply' while the body shows the specific thread topic being replied to.
A documentation leaf whose <title> is the bare action 'Installing' while the body identifies the specific product and section ('CLI Tools - Installation').

pages.scenario: A finished quarterly-revenue investor-relations article (masthead, prose, management quotes, a revenue-by-segment data table) whose <title> is the literal Adobe Dreamweaver new-document default 'Untitled Document'.
pages.mechanism: F25 sub-class (a): authoring-tool default title. The <title> text node is 'Untitled Document', which announces the absence of a title and identifies nothing about the Q3-revenue subject; AT/tab/bookmark/search-result readers cannot distinguish it from any other 'Untitled Document'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe document-title / WAVE / Lighthouse / ACT 2779a5 only verify a non-empty <title> exists. 'Untitled Document' is non-empty, valid UTF-8 and a grammatical noun phrase, so it passes every presence/format heuristic. Recognizing it as an authoring-tool default that means no-title requires semantic knowledge a checker lacks.

pages.scenario: A shipped Vite + React single-page app rendering a real 'New Engineer Onboarding Checklist' HR console view, whose document <title> is left at the build scaffold default 'Vite + React' and is never updated on route change.
pages.mechanism: F25 sub-class (c) + SPA dynamic-state: the <title> is the build tool's name, not the page's. The inline script never sets document.title and the SPA never updates it per view, so every route reports 'Vite + React' to AT and the tab, identifying tooling not content and failing to distinguish views served from one URL.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'Vite + React' is a non-empty valid title so document-title / 2779a5 pass on the served HTML; scanners also evaluate the initial DOM and do not model that the SPA never updates document.title per view. Knowing it is a generator default describing the framework, not the onboarding page, is semantic judgment.

citation.quote: In cases such as Single Page Applications (SPAs), where various distinct pages/views are all nominally served from the same URI and the content of the page is changed dynamically, the title of the page should also be changed dynamically to reflect the content or topic of the current view.

pages.scenario: A complete Returns & Refunds policy page (breadcrumb, h1, effective date, return steps, refund timing, FAQ definition list) whose <title> is the unfilled CMS placeholder 'TODO: add page title'.

pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The string is non-empty, valid, sentence-case, and even contains the dictionary token 'title', so document-title / 2779a5 pass. No linter knows 'TODO: add page title' is an unfilled template token rather than a real title; distinguishing residue from content is semantic recognition.

pages.scenario: A finished field-research brief (descriptive h1 on riparian-buffer stream-temperature study, metadata list, executive summary, key findings, recommendation, methods) whose <title> is the source filename 'report.html' — F25's own literal example.
pages.mechanism: F25 sub-class (c): a filename not descriptive in its own right. A docs generator used the filename as <title> when no front-matter title was supplied, emitting 'report.html' with the extension. The string identifies a file ('report' of what?), not a subject, and the '.html' is machine residue; it does not distinguish this brief from any other report.html.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'report.html' is non-empty and valid so document-title / 2779a5 pass; a scanner cannot tell a non-descriptive filename ('report.html') from a genuine terse title ('Report 2024') since both are short strings. Recognizing '.html' as a filename extension signalling residue, and 'report' as non-identifying alone, is semantic judgment.

pages.scenario: Long-form local-news article (~600 words) on the Cedar Falls City Council adopting a $214M municipal budget after a contested vote on police and parks funding. The page is a rich news layout (promo banner, masthead, section nav, article, sidebar with most-read/ad/newsletter, footer), but the <title> 'Summer Sale — 20% Off Annual Subscriptions | Cedar Falls Tribune' is lifted from the top rotating subscription promo banner — a peripheral marketing block, not the budget story that is the page's primary topic.
pages.mechanism: F25 limb (b): the <title> is non-empty and accurately describes a real, present PERIPHERAL block (.promo-banner), but does not identify the OVERALL/primary content (the article#hl headline about the $214M budget vote). A screen reader announces the page as a sale promo; in tabs/history/bookmarks/search the budget story is filed under marketing copy, and two different stories could share the identical promo title, so it also fails to distinguish the page.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core document-title, WAVE, and Lighthouse only verify a non-empty <title> exists; the title's words ('Summer Sale', 'Subscriptions') literally appear in the .promo-banner DOM, so even a keyword-presence heuristic finds a match. No tool models which region is the page's primary topic versus a promo rail, and none compares the title against the dominant content region. Deciding the budget article — not the sale banner — is the page's subject requires human reading comprehension and a sense of visual/semantic prominence.

pages.scenario: A food-blog recipe page whose dominant main column is a complete recipe for 'Brown Butter Miso Chocolate Chip Cookies' (full ingredient list + five-step numbered method). The <title> 'Sign up for our newsletter — sweetcrumb.kitchen' is the heading of the sidebar newsletter-signup card — a peripheral conversion widget — rather than the recipe that is the page's subject.
pages.mechanism: F25 limb (b): the <title> names the sidebar newsletter widget heading (aside .card.nl > h2) instead of the primary recipe (main.recipe > h1#rtitle). The title is non-empty and its words are present in the DOM, but it identifies a peripheral widget, not the overall content. Because every recipe page carries the same widget, the title also fails to distinguish the page — a screen reader announces 'Sign up for our newsletter' for what is actually the cookie recipe.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <title> is present and non-empty so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass; the phrase 'Sign up for our newsletter' appears verbatim in the sidebar DOM, so token-overlap between title and page text scores a match. No tool can tell that the recipe — not the newsletter card — is the page's primary topic, which requires recognizing the recipe as the visually/semantically dominant region and reading its meaning.

pages.scenario: An ATS job-posting page whose entire main column is a specific posting: 'Senior Backend Engineer (Payments)' at Northwind Robotics (role summary, responsibilities, requirements, compensation, Apply button). The <title> 'Building robots that give people their time back. — Northwind Robotics' is the company's generic mission-statement tagline that appears only in the footer — a peripheral brand block — and is emitted as the title of every posting in the set.
pages.mechanism: F25 'same title for each page' + limb (b): the <title> is the global footer tagline (footer > p.tagline), not the posting headline (h1#jtitle). It is non-empty but describes the company brand, not THIS job, and is duplicated across every posting — so a screen-reader user hears every Northwind job tab announced identically and cannot distinguish the Senior Backend Engineer role from any other open posting.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <title> is non-empty so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass; the tagline's words appear verbatim in the footer so token-overlap heuristics match. Detecting that every posting carries the SAME tagline-title requires crawling and comparing multiple pages, which single-URL scanners never do; and judging that the title fails to name the specific job requires reading the posting and understanding it is the page's primary subject.

pages.scenario: Online-banking statement view. The body is unambiguously the December 2005 statement for Account 1234-5678 (H1, statement-period metadata 1-31 Dec 2005, every transaction date 02-30 Dec 2005, closing-balance row, breadcrumb current page, PDF download filename ...-2005-12-..., footer). The <title> reads 'Meridian Bank — November 2005 statement for Account 1234-5678' — the statement template carried over the prior month's title. Mirrors the WCAG Understanding bank example run in reverse: same bank/document-type/account, plausible month, one stale identifier (the month).
pages.mechanism: F25 descriptiveness limb (Trusted Tester 12.B): a present, on-topic <title> names a DIFFERENT (sibling) statement than the page's content. The month is the identifier that distinguishes monthly statements in a set; the title's month (November) contradicts the body's true period (December), so within the set it neither identifies this page nor distinguishes it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse verify only that a <title> exists and is non-empty (ACT 2779a5). The title is valid, non-empty, unique, human-sounding, and shares vocabulary with the body ('statement','Account 1234-5678', a month name), so a keyword-overlap heuristic also passes it. Catching it requires extracting the body's true period (December — from H1, period metadata, transaction dates, download filename) and noticing the title's month is the prior instance. No linter knows November != December in a way that matters.

pages.scenario: A nonprofit cloned last year's annual-gala page to build this year's. The body is updated throughout to the 2026 event — an inline-SVG hero date banner reading 'SATURDAY 14 MARCH 2026' (with correct aria-label), the 'This year at a glance' date, the 2026 honoree, 2026 ticket prices, 'Program for the evening of 14 March 2026', and footer. AT receives two contradictory year signals and the orientation-authoritative one (the title) is wrong; within an annually recurring set it fails to distinguish this edition.

pages.scenario: A developer-docs release-notes page built by a static-site generator from markdown front matter. The body is unambiguously the v4.2.0 notes: the version <select> shows 'v4.2.0 (current)' selected, the H1 reads 'Release notes — Quartzdb v4.2.0', the release date and package line read quartzdb@4.2.0, the install snippet pins quartzdb@4.2.0, and every changelog heading/item is scoped to 4.2.0. The <title> reads 'Release notes — v4.1.0 · Quartzdb Documentation' — the version was bumped everywhere except the page's front-matter title: field. The body deliberately also MENTIONS 4.1.0 in context ('Upgrading from 4.1.0 to 4.2.0', 'regression present since 4.1.0').
pages.mechanism: F25 descriptiveness limb, sharpened: the title's version (4.1.0) is not absent from the body — it appears as a REFERENCED prior version, not the page's SUBJECT version (4.2.0, set by the H1, selected version control, release date, install pin). The title names a different release than the page documents; among versioned release-notes pages it fails to distinguish this page.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm a present, non-empty, product-qualified, on-topic title (ACT 2779a5). A keyword-overlap heuristic is actively fooled: '4.1.0' appears in BOTH the title and the body (upgrade/regression sentences), so naive title-vs-content overlap scores it consistent. Determining the page's true subject version requires distinguishing the subject (H1 + selected version control + install pin) from referenced versions — a semantic distinction no linter or overlap metric makes.

pages.scenario: A pharmacy patient-portal 'refill ready' confirmation. After a dose increase the patient has two Lisinopril prescriptions: the discontinued 10 mg (Rx 4471829) and the active 20 mg (Rx 4471830). This page is the 20 mg refill: the H1, patient/Rx subheading (Rx 4471830), a bilingual EN/Simplified-Chinese image-of-text dispensed label (inline SVG, aria-label 'Lisinopril 20 mg ... Rx 4471830'), the strength field (20 mg), directions, pickup line ('your 20 mg refill'), an explicit note that the 10 mg was discontinued, and footer all say 20 mg / Rx 4471830. The <title> reads 'Refill ready: Lisinopril 10 mg — Rx 4471829 | BayCare Pharmacy', built from a stale cached prescription summary naming the discontinued strength.
pages.mechanism: F25 descriptiveness limb (safety-critical): the <title> names the discontinued 10 mg / Rx 4471829 while the body — including the image-of-text label's aria-label that AT reads — establishes the refill is 20 mg / Rx 4471830. Strength is what distinguishes this confirmation from the sibling Rx; a patient trusting the announced title is told the wrong (old) dose, risking the wrong medication strength.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse verify only a present, non-empty, pharmacy-qualified, on-topic title (ACT 2779a5). A keyword-overlap tool passes it because title and body share 'Refill ready','Lisinopril','BayCare Pharmacy','Rx','mg' — and the body even mentions 10 mg / Rx 4471829 in the discontinuation note, so naive overlap finds the title's tokens present and scores it consistent. The deciding facts (subject = 20 mg / Rx 4471830; 10 mg = referenced discontinued prior) live in the H1, the SVG label's accessible name, the strength field, and the note's semantics, none of which a checker parses or reconciles against the title.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary variant. A municipal transit timetable, which ships as a set of near-identical sibling pages (Weekday / Saturday / Sunday & Holiday) — exactly the situation that breeds stale copy-paste titles. Here the author got the specific instance RIGHT: the <title> reads 'Route 12 Riverside — Saturday Schedule | Metro Transit', and the body — breadcrumb current page, H1, day-selector (Saturday marked aria-current=page), service note ('Saturday service runs every 30 minutes...'), table caption ('Saturday departures — Route 12 Riverside'), 'All times are Saturdays only', and footer — is unambiguously the Saturday schedule for the same route. Title and body share the route family and timetable vocabulary AND agree on the one critical identifier (the service day).
pages.mechanism: No F25 failure: the title is present AND identifies the contents AND distinguishes the page within its set of sibling timetables — the service day in the title matches the service day throughout the body. This is the in-family MATCH the five failing cases are contrasted against, proving the judgment under test is 'does the title's specific instance match the body's?', not 'does a title exist?'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Irrelevant to the verdict but instructive: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse would report PASS here for the same shallow reason they wrongly PASS the failing cases — a present, non-empty title (ACT 2779a5). They cannot see whether the title's service day agrees with the body's. The correct PASS here comes only from a human (or model) cross-check succeeding; the identical cross-check fails in case-01 through case-05. This case confirms a detector keys on the title-vs-body identifier MATCH rather than on surface presence or on mere structural similarity to the failing cases.

finalReport.summary:
I have the scoring data I need (final tally is authoritative). Let me write the prose summary directly, as instructed not to recompute.

The ACT test suite for SC 2.4.2 (rules like `2779a5`, "HTML page has non-empty title") covers only Limb (a): the mechanical presence of a non-empty `<title>` element. It is silent on Limb (b) — whether that title actually *describes the topic or purpose* of the page — because describing-ness is a human judgment that no deterministic rule can adjudicate. So a page can pass every ACT check while carrying a title that identifies nothing, describes the wrong thing, or fails to orient the user. The five uncovered aspects target exactly this Limb (b) blind spot: non-identifying artifact titles (F25 — authoring-tool defaults, unfilled placeholders, filename/code strings); titles that describe a secondary block instead of the page's primary topic on mixed-content pages; stale copy-paste titles that name the right subject family but the wrong specific instance (date, version, account); titles too generic to distinguish one page from its siblings in a set (site-name-only or template-shared inner pages); and titles that read fine in-page but lose meaning out of context, failing G88/G127 collection-position orientation.

The augmented corpus now covers all five aspects with valid human-judgment pages above the five-page threshold: non-identifying artifact titles at 7 valid, and the remaining four — secondary-not-primary topic, stale wrong-instance, too-generic-to-distinguish, and loses-meaning-out-of-context — each at 6 valid. No aspect is short of the 5-valid-page bar, so none requires regeneration; every Limb (b) facet has sufficient coverage.
